## Preliminary Incident Report
We recognize that Google Cloud services are critical to your organization, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption this incident may have caused to your business. We are working to address the root cause and prevent this from occurring in the future.
Please note, this information is based on our best knowledge at the time of posting and is subject to change as our investigation continues. A final Incident Report with preventative actions will be posted once our investigation is complete.
If you have experienced impact outside of what is listed below, please reach out to Google Cloud Support using [**https\://cloud.google.com/support**](https://cloud.google.com/support).
## Date/Time of the Issue
Incident Start:19 Oct 2026 23:00 US/Pacific / 20 Oct 2026 07:00 BST
Incident End: 20 Oct 2026 05:10 US/Pacific / 20 Oct 2026 13:10 BST
Duration: 6 hours, 10 minutes
## Summary
On Monday, 19 October 2026 (Tuesday, 20 October BST), multiple Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions, elevated error rates, Application Programming Interface (API) timeouts, and processing latency for a duration of 6 hours and 10 minutes. The disruption was triggered by an electrical power interruption at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, which temporarily took physical host servers, network routing hardware, and storage systems offline. This subsequently caused secondary failover and queuing delays across unimpacted regional infrastructure. 
## Preliminary Root Cause
The incident was triggered when a power grid disruption occurred at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b. To maintain continuous power during the disruption, automatic transfer to facility backup power systems was triggered immediately. The facility load was transferred to the Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery banks during the start up sequence of on-site emergency diesel generators. The Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) automation system (both primary and backup PLCs) failed to initiate the logical automatic start/transfer operations of the generators, preventing backup generators from assuming the load. When UPS battery reserves were depleted, physical host servers, network switching fabric, and local storage arrays dedicated to europe-west2-b lost power and went offline.
The sequence of events leading to customer impact was as follows:
* At 22:53 US/Pacific (20 Oct, 06:53 BST), an electrical power disruption occurred at the datacenter facility hosting availability zone europe-west2-b, and a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) startup fault prevented facility emergency generators from assuming the electrical load. Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted, starting at 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct, 07:00 BST).
* When the physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in europe-west2-b lost power, it caused instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* Regional traffic-routing mechanisms and client applications initiated automated failover toward available infrastructure in adjacent availability zones within the region.
* Cross-zone remote procedure calls from regional service control planes directed to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone encountered timeouts, causing initial job submission stalls and API latency spikes.
* The sudden influx of redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers, and compute workloads saturated available compute slots and processing capacity in other availability zones, creating elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions, and intermittent 500 and 503 API errors across the region.
Google engineers have begun a full root cause analysis (RCA) and will provide additional information once it is available.
## Remediation
Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers at 23:08 US/Pacific on 19 Oct (20 Oct, 07:08 BST), which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery:
* **Traffic Isolation:** Google engineers isolated the offline availability zone (europe-west2-b) by adjusting regional service routing away from the affected infrastructure, preventing cross-zone client requests from timing out against offline endpoints.
* **Workload Reprioritization and Resource Safeguards:** Engineers adjusted scheduler allocations and capacity limits across unimpacted infrastructure to prioritize active customer reservations, reduce resource contention on execution slots, and relieve queue backlogs for regional workloads.
* **Power Grid Restoration:** On-site facility engineers conducted graceful restoration of a stable utility power feed once utility supply was back, within 1 hour. Following this, they focused and completed a reset and tested the emergency backup generator automation controllers to restore facility power.
* **Progressive Infrastructure Re-activation:** Google engineers systematically restarted core Google Cloud infrastructure and services.
* **Controlled Traffic Re-admission:** Once system health and storage integrity were verified, engineers executed gradual, controlled traffic re-admission back to zone europe-west2-b allowing accumulated job backlogs to clear smoothly.
By 05:10 US/Pacific on Tuesday, 20 Oct(13:10 BST), service availability had recovered for the vast majority of customer workloads, and resolution for most of the customers across Google Cloud Platform services in the region was confirmed. Following the recovery of a small tail of remaining isolated workloads, the closure notification for the incident was posted by 07:03 US/Pacific (15:03 BST).
## Description of Impact
Between Monday, 19 Oct 2026, 23:00 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) and Tuesday, 20 October 2026, 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST), customers utilizing Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions across two consecutive phases, lasting a total duration of 6 hours, 10 minutes.
During the initial phase from 23:00 to 04:29 US/Pacific (07:00 to 12:29 BST) (duration 5 hours, 29 minutes), customers experienced elevated error rates, API timeouts, and processing delays until most Google Cloud Platform services recovered.
Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances experienced a longer recovery tail. By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new Virtual Machine creation resumed and by 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine Virtual Machines were in a healthy state. Any remaining customers that were experiencing Virtual Machine problems were directed to file a customer support issue as per normal procedure.
While the physical power outage was isolated strictly to datacenter facilities in europe-west2-b, some customers running workloads in unimpacted zones (europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c) or across regional architectures also experienced unexpected impact.
The primary causes were 1\) instantaneous demand surges on unimpacted compute capacity and 2\) synchronous control-plane validation dependencies across zonal boundaries. Affected products included: BigQuery, Looker, Google Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Regional Persistent Disk, and Cloud SQL. These services experienced unexpected degradation and failover issues driven by sudden compute capacity exhaustion from surging demand, and control-plane API timeouts waiting on validations from the offline zone.
Workloads and resources hosted entirely within europe-west2-b became unreachable. Data storage services with failover capability such as Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Memorystore for Redis, and Cloud Bigtable failed over into nearby unimpacted zones during the europe-west2-b outage. Multi-zonal and regional services that spanned across the europe-west2 region experienced elevated latency, transient API errors (such as HTTP 500 and 503 errors), and task admission queuing as failover traffic concentrated onto unimpacted regional resources and cross-zone calls to offline components timed out. Storage write operations in the region experienced a transient error rate during the initial failover period, and regional query admission queues temporarily peaked before rapidly subsiding as capacity re-balanced.

## Incident Report
### **Summary**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 (Tuesday, 20 Oct BST), a data center facility that hosts europe-west2-b, experienced an external electrical power disruption. This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. As traffic was redirected to alternative cloud regions or unaffected zones within europe-west2 cloud region, these workloads experienced transient latency and elevated errors affecting services across europe-west2. 
The primary impact was mitigated after 6 hours 8 minutes.
### **Root Cause**
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—meaning the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Static Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide 5 minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened and key-interlocked (Locked Out Tagged Out) to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while repairs were conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.  
When the primary utility feed A was lost, the facility’s generator plant failed to receive a signal to automatically start and take critical load due to a design voltage-sensing and misconfiguration in the PLCs. The facility's static UPS battery banks carried the critical load as designed until their battery reserves depleted resulting in a complete power loss across data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed B breaker. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the feeder before commanding a generator start. As the utility feed B remained energized upstream, both PLCs sensed live upstream voltage on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.;
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be exhausted before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.
After the power loss was initially detected, Google engineers began work to mitigate failover failures and prepare service recovery. Upon restoration of the utility source, UPS and generator capabilities, they began the process to re-enable services in europe-west2-b.

Facility load continued to be supported by UPS battery banks until the batteries were depleted.
* **19 Oct 23:00 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:00 BST)** **Impact start -** As battery backups were exhausted, physical host servers, local storage infrastructure, and network aggregation hardware in availability zone europe-west2-b lost power, causing instances, database replicas, and worker nodes in that zone to become immediately unreachable.
* **19 Oct 23:04 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:04 BST) -** Google engineers were alerted to the disruption via automated monitoring systems and probers, which detected elevated API error ratios, job submission timeouts, and loss of infrastructure reachability in zone europe-west2-b. Engineering teams immediately mobilized to isolate the affected infrastructure and commence recovery.
* **19 Oct 23:09 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:09 BST) -** Regional traffic-routing mechanisms and client applications initiated automated failover toward available infrastructure in adjacent availability zones within the region. * Cross-zone remote procedure calls from regional service control planes directed to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone encountered timeouts, causing initial job submission stalls and API latency spikes. * The sudden influx of redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers, and compute workloads saturated available compute slots and processing capacity in other availability zones, creating elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions, and intermittent 500 and 503 API errors across the region. * **Traffic Isolation:** Google engineers isolated the offline availability zone (europe-west2-b) by adjusting regional service routing away from the affected infrastructure, preventing cross-zone client requests from timing out against offline endpoints. * **Workload Reprioritization and Resource Safeguards:** Engineers adjusted scheduler allocations and capacity limits across unimpacted infrastructure to prioritize active customer reservations, reduce resource contention on execution slots, and relieve queue backlogs for regional workloads.
* **19 Oct 23:54 US/Pacific (20 Oct 07:54 BST) Utility Power Restoration** **\-** Power supply from the standby utility source was restored and power restoration to the data hall began.
* **20 Oct 00:20 US/Pacific (08:20 BST) Datahall Power Restoration** **\-** Utility power was re-established to the datahalls. Mains utility power normalized; power feed to data hall verified. Following this, the site operations and engineering teams focused on and completed a reset and tested the emergency backup generator automation controllers to restore facility power.
* **20 Oct 00:40 US/Pacific (08:40 BST)** **\-** Clusters began to recover, cluster manager systems started rescheduling compute jobs. 
* **20 Oct 00:45 US/Pacific (08:45 BST) \-** Network devices were back online. 
* **20 Oct 00:50 US/Pacific (08:50 BST) \-** Due to the immediacy of power loss, storage devices with unclean shutdowns began recovery. Responders recognized this and chose not to restore services that would otherwise make this worse. Because of the large volume of storage devices involved, this process required a substantial period to finish prior to restoring service to customers.
* **20 Oct 03:13 US/Pacific (11:06 BST)** **\-** Power redundancy was verified and the storage infrastructure was sufficiently restored to prepare the initiation of controlled traffic re-admission. The remaining storage systems continued recovery operations.
* **20 Oct 03:45 US/Pacific (11:45 BST) Controlled Traffic Re-admission** **\-** Once system health and storage integrity were verified, engineers executed gradual, controlled traffic re-admission back to zone europe-west2-b allowing accumulated job backlogs to clear smoothly.

* **20 Oct 05:08 US/Pacific (13:08 BST) Majority Workload Recovery** **\-** GCE virtual machines were 99.5% operational and healthy, and creating new VMs was fully supported. Service availability was restored for most customer workloads, with resolution confirmed for the majority of users across Google Cloud Platform services in the region. Following the recovery of a small tail of remaining isolated workloads, the closure notification for the incident was posted by 07:03 US/Pacific (15:03 BST).
Google is committed to preventing a repeat of this issue in the future and is completing the following actions:

* Generator confidence testing * Full generator load transfer tests with utility power cutover of the active utility feed. Test automatic startup of generators through PLC signals within the backup battery timer and detailed review of backup procedures **\[Completed on 20 Oct and 26 Oct (full critical load transfer test including updated EOPs)\]** * Full generator load transfer tests in coordination with the primary utility source feeds (A and B) after restoration work completed by the primary utility provider. **\[Estimated Completion Date 31 Oct\]**
* PLC configuration fix  * Reconfigured and validated the PLC after the outage on 20 Oct and then again on 26 Oct **\[Completed 26 Oct\]** * Google engineers to work in collaboration with the facility vendor teams to perform a comprehensive PLC code review and system resiliency to multiple failure scenarios. **\[Estimated Completion Date (prior to generator transfer test) estimated 31 Oct\]** * Validate PLC telemetry once primary utility feed A and B lineup is restored. **\[Estimated Completion Date 31 Oct\]** * Validate global PLC configurations at all global sites with similar topologies and PLC manufacturers, to ensure confidence in automatic generator starts. **\[Estimated Completion Date 15 Nov\]**
* Emergency Operating Procedures (EOP) documentation update: * Comprehensive update to the EOP for site’s response to unexpected loss of active utility source. Update includes \- manual steps to attempt to restore active utility feed, manual restart of generators and manual transfer to other utility sources within the UPS battery run time. **\[Completed 26 Oct\]** * Ensure updated EOP is practiced twice per shift by on-site facility team. **\[Completed 24 Oct and checked with Google DC Operations daily\]**
* Strengthen change management:  * Freeze planned maintenance activities at other sites with similar topologies, and implement elevated approvals and reviews for data center configuration changes which are outside their standard designs. **\[Estimated Completion Date 30 Oct\]**
**Cloud Service Action Items:**
* **Communications Enhancement:** Bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.
* **Platform Testing:** Expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.
### **Detailed Description of Impact**

The unavailability of those resources scoped to a zone that undergoes disruption is working within the design of a zonally-scoped system. 1) Instantaneous demand surges on neighboring zones (a and c) and
2) Control-plane dependencies across zonal boundaries

Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances as well as products that rely on Compute Engine experienced a longer recovery due to action taken by responders in order to prevent data loss. Once storage stabilized, engineers brought VMs and zonal disks in the zone back online between 04:01 US/Pacific (12:01 BST) and 04:29 US/Pacific (12:29 BST). By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new VM creation resumed, and by 05:08 US/Pacific (13:08 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine VM were in a healthy state. The follow-up actions focus on preventing a recurrence and on making our clusters recover from an unplanned power loss more quickly and safely. We are also expanding our regular disaster-recovery testing for full cluster power-loss scenarios to validate end-to-end Compute Engine recovery.

We are investigating additional signals to incorporate into our failure detection capabilities for Regional Persistent Disk, so that should this sequence recur, Regional Persistent Disk can differentiate this case from the more typical zonal outage scenarios. Engineering teams have updated job provisioning to eliminate the dependency on autoscaling and are enhancing isolation mechanisms for the job server to ensure that future zonal disruptions are contained.

The team is working on mechanisms to detect cases when the control plane and data plane get out of sync, then reconcile them so that the system can automatically recover.

**Impact:**
During the power disruption, the Apigee X runtime in the region returned elevated HTTP 5xx errors for 7 hours and 19 minutes. The engineering team has already audited the Apigee fleet to rebalance unevenly spread instances without downtime, and added monitoring to alert if datastore replicas drift across zones. Moving forward, the team will modify Apigee X to strictly enforce that every instance's three datastore replicas always run in three different zones. Additionally, the team is improving alert handling practices to help engineers better focus on affected services during similar outages.

**Impact:**
During the power disruption, Apigee Edge clusters that had a single node in the affected zone successfully auto-recovered once power was restored. However, clusters with multiple nodes in the affected zone experienced extended recovery times. The automated node replacement system didn't handle multiple nodes going down simultaneously. Furthermore, during this manual recovery, some virtual machines experienced a timeout when attempting to reach external OS repositories, causing them to boot with an older binary version and further delaying full restoration.
**Next Steps:**
The engineering team will implement retries and scope repository updates to prevent pre-hook timeouts when reaching external OS repositories during the boot process. The team is also investigating further multiple-node failure scenario resilience improvements.

Cloud Bigtable behaved as expected during the europe-west2-b power outage. All single-cluster instances located in europe-west2-b experienced expected zonal unavailability while the zone lost power and recovered. Multi-cluster instances configured with High Availability (HA) routing automatically failed over to healthy replica clusters in other zones where replica clusters and the control plane remained available with sufficient capacity to absorb the failover load.

1) Instantaneous demand surges on neighboring zones (a and c) and
2) Control-plane dependencies across zonal boundaries

During this incident, however, some of these failover attempts were unsuccessful due to capacity constraints and difficulty in replicating the underlying storage mechanism.

Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances as well as products that rely on Compute Engine experienced a longer recovery due to action taken by responders in order to prevent data loss. Once storage stabilized, engineers brought VMs and zonal disks in the zone back online between 04:01 US/Pacific (12:01 BST) and 04:29 US/Pacific (12:29 BST). By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new VM creation resumed, and by 05:08 US/Pacific (13:08 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine VM were in a healthy state. **Impact:**

The resolution of the main impact was completed within 6 hours and 8 minutes.
## Root Cause
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders (A and B) terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide approximately five minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.
Following the loss of primary utility feed A, a voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load. Consequently, static UPS battery banks sustained the critical load as intended until their reserves were used up, leading to a loss of power across the data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed breakers. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the line side of the feeder before commanding a generator start. At the time of the power event on 19 Oct 2026, the Utility feed B remained energized upstream while its incomer feed was in open position. Consequently, the active and standby master PLCs, which were running identical control logic, sensed live voltage from feed B through shared upstream sensors on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action due to the live upstream voltage reading on feed B. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be used up before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.

## Incident Report
### **Summary**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 (Tuesday, 20 Oct BST), a data center facility that hosts europe-west2-b, experienced an external electrical power disruption. This resulted in service unavailability for workloads located in this zone. As traffic was redirected to alternative cloud regions or unaffected zones within europe-west2 cloud region, these workloads experienced transient latency and elevated errors affecting services across europe-west2. 
The primary impact was mitigated after 6 hours 8 minutes.
### **Root Cause**
**Facility architecture and background:**
The data center facility in the UK region hosts Cloud clusters serving the europe-west2-b zone, which form part of the multi-zonal europe-west2 Cloud region. The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture—meaning the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load—backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC).
Primary utility power is supplied to the facility via two independent feeders (A and B), supplemented by a standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events. The two high-voltage primary feeders terminate at separate primary intake switchboards capable of closed-loop operation if either board is taken offline. Switching between the primary and standby utility providers utilizes open transitions and key interlocks to prevent parallel connections across sources.
Static Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) battery systems provide 5 minutes of autonomous runtime. This bridge power ensures uninterrupted operation while the PLC detects utility undervoltage events, initiates diesel generator startup, synchronizes the generators, and transfers the site load.
Prior to the utility disruption, the facility had been placed in a temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture on the primary utility. Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened and key-interlocked (Locked Out Tagged Out) to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026. Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while repairs were conducted on the B feeder pathway.
**Root Cause:**
On Monday, 19 Oct 2026 at 22:53 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 06:53 BST), the primary utility provider experienced an outage on primary utility feed A, caused by an external underground cable fault on the utility network outside the data center facility.  
When the primary utility feed A was lost, the facility’s generator plant failed to receive a signal to automatically start and take critical load due to a design voltage-sensing and misconfiguration in the PLCs. The facility's static UPS battery banks carried the critical load as designed until their battery reserves depleted resulting in a complete power loss across data halls.
The investigation of the PLC configuration identified the root cause as a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position for both utility feeders. Instead, the PLC undervoltage sensing inputs were wired upstream (line side) of the isolated utility feed B breaker. The PLC was programmed to verify whether voltage was present on the feeder before commanding a generator start. As the utility feed B remained energized upstream, both PLCs sensed live upstream voltage on the disconnected path. As a result, the PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant.;
The onsite facilities team attempted to execute a remote load transfer via the PLC; however, the system inhibited the action. Recognizing that the UPS battery reserves would be exhausted before further remote operations could be resolved, the team transferred the facility load to the standby utility source, restoring the critical load that was lost once batteries depleted during this process.
Once utility power was restored via the standby utility source, and UPS batteries started recharging, the onsite facility teams and OEM vendors reconfigured and validated PLC functionality on both undervoltage and breaker status.
After the power loss was initially detected, Google engineers began work to mitigate failover failures and prepare service recovery. Upon restoration of the utility source, UPS and generator capabilities, they began the process to re-enable services in europe-west2-b.

The Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) automation system (both primary and backup PLCs) failed to initiate the logical automatic start/transfer operations of the generators, preventing backup generators from assuming the load. ## Description of Impact
Between Monday, 19 Oct 2026, 23:00 US/Pacific (Tuesday, 20 Oct 2026, 07:00 BST) and Tuesday, 20 October 2026, 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST), customers utilizing Google Cloud Platform services in the europe-west2 region experienced service disruptions across two consecutive phases, lasting a total duration of 6 hours, 10 minutes.
During the initial phase from 23:00 to 04:29 US/Pacific (07:00 to 12:29 BST) (duration 5 hours, 29 minutes), customers experienced elevated error rates, API timeouts, and processing delays until most Google Cloud Platform services recovered.
Following platform service restoration, some customer workloads running on Compute Engine instances experienced a longer recovery tail. By 04:46 US/Pacific (12:46 BST) new Virtual Machine creation resumed and by 05:10 US/Pacific (13:10 BST) over 99% of Compute Engine Virtual Machines were in a healthy state. Any remaining customers that were experiencing Virtual Machine problems were directed to file a customer support issue as per normal procedure.
While the physical power outage was isolated strictly to datacenter facilities in europe-west2-b, some customers running workloads in unimpacted zones (europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c) or across regional architectures also experienced unexpected impact.
The primary causes were 1\) instantaneous demand surges on unimpacted compute capacity and 2\) synchronous control-plane validation dependencies across zonal boundaries. Affected products included: BigQuery, Looker, Google Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Regional Persistent Disk, and Cloud SQL. These services experienced unexpected degradation and failover issues driven by sudden compute capacity exhaustion from surging demand, and control-plane API timeouts waiting on validations from the offline zone.
Workloads and resources hosted entirely within europe-west2-b became unreachable. Data storage services with failover capability such as Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Memorystore for Redis, and Cloud Bigtable failed over into nearby unimpacted zones during the europe-west2-b outage. Multi-zonal and regional services that spanned across the europe-west2 region experienced elevated latency, transient API errors (such as HTTP 500 and 503 errors), and task admission queuing as failover traffic concentrated onto unimpacted regional resources and cross-zone calls to offline components timed out. Storage write operations in the region experienced a transient error rate during the initial failover period, and regional query admission queues temporarily peaked before rapidly subsiding as capacity re-balanced.
